sections.html:
• Name: Whisker shrimp
  • Other names: Indian Whisker Shrimp, Thailand Ghost shrimp, Glass shrimp, Ghost shrimp, Riceland prawn
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: Medium–Difficult
  • KH: 1–8
  • TDS: 100–300
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: aggressive
  • Colour: translucent

In the aquarium hobby, Whisker shrimp are often mislabeled as common Ghost shrimp (Palaemonetes paludosus). Compared with Ghost shrimp, Whisker shrimp have longer front legs and larger front claws (almost as long as the body), while Ghost shrimp claws are much smaller. Many Whisker shrimp develop a darker colour and have brown to black stripes on the front body, whereas Ghost shrimp remain transparent with 2 small red dots on the tail and red to orange bands on the legs and feelers. Whisker shrimp reach up to 6 cm, Ghost shrimp up to 5 cm.

Many young Macrobrachium look like Ghost shrimp before they grow huge, and these are also sometimes called Whisker shrimp, which creates more confusion.

Whisker shrimp are among the most abundant and widespread shrimp species in Peninsular Malaysia, Thailand and Myanmar, as well as southern China and Java, Indonesia. They are also one of the most common species in Laos.
They are common in shallow waters (1–2 metres or less) and live in fresh waters such as lakes, ponds, canals, paddy fields and swamps. They can also be found in slow-flowing streams and rivers.

Whisker shrimp move a lot, so the tank should be big enough for them to roam and hide. The absolute minimum for a few shrimp (1 male and 1–2 females) is 40 litres. Overstocking can lead to health problems and aggression, especially with more than one male. They are voracious eaters and produce a lot of bioload. They tend to climb out of the aquarium, so a lid is advised.

Whisker shrimp are very easy to care for, even for beginners. The tank must be fully cycled; they cannot survive in an uncycled tank or during cycling, and are susceptible to ammonia, nitrites and nitrates. Check water parameters weekly and do water changes to keep nitrate down.

If keeping several, make most of them females: one male to about 1–2 females reduces aggression.

Provide plenty of hiding places, which is also crucial for moulting, as cannibalism after moulting can be a big problem. They appreciate leaves, rocks, wood, PVC pipes, etc. Acclimate them slowly, about 2–3 hours. They do not tolerate copper-based medications.

Whisker shrimp do not really need light, so lighting should suit the plants. They can be kept on any substrate. There are no special filter requirements; sponge or matten filters are recommended for small tanks as they are cheap, easy to maintain and provide surfaces to graze on, and this species will not tear the sponge apart. For bigger tanks, hang-on-back or canister filters are needed.

They are detritivore-omnivores, feeding mainly on phytoplankton, biofilm, detritus, insects and molluscs. In the aquarium they eat almost anything: dead plants, leaf litter, blanched vegetables, flakes, sinking pellets and wafers, dead and dying fish, shrimp, bloodworms, dried gammarus, brine shrimp, daphnia and snails. They are greedy and easy to overfeed. Feed rations that last 1–2 hours at most, then remove uneaten food. They may eat algae when very hungry but are not efficient algae eaters.

Whisker shrimp have an aggressive temperament. They will attack small prey such as dwarf shrimp, snails and small fish, so they are a questionable choice for a peaceful community tank. They are not very social; males bully each other over territory and will fight members of their own species. Macrobrachium are territorial, aggressive and cannibalistic. They are nocturnal and become hyperactive towards dusk. They are fast and can jump.

Tankmates: large or aggressive fish should be avoided, and small fish (such as neon tetras and guppies) and bottom-dwelling fish may disappear over time. Dwarf shrimp and snails are best avoided, and even Amano shrimp may be caught. Avoid crayfish (except perhaps Cambarellus), other freshwater crabs and frogs.

They are not very plant-damaging in most cases, but some keepers report them eating tender plants such as mosses.
Females are longer than males. A greenish saddle in a female shows eggs ripening in the ovaries.

Whisker shrimp can breed in freshwater setups but produce larvae, not miniature shrimp. Fecundity is around 59–393 eggs, depending on female size. The female carries the eggs for 3–4 weeks (depending on temperature); after hatching, larvae take another 2–3 weeks to become young shrimp. Larvae cannot tolerate poor water quality (ammonia, nitrites, nitrates). A cycled rearing tank with the same water parameters is recommended to avoid adult aggression.

Feed larvae with newly hatched brine shrimp and artificial fish-larvae food (e.g. 50 or 100-micron golden pearls), daily and ideally twice, without fouling the water. Larvae do not recover from earlier starvation.

Macrobrachium is a genus of about 240 species in the family Palaemonidae; "macro" means long and "brachium" means arm. Whisker shrimp are semitransparent with brown to black stripes on the front body, a straight rostrum, very long front arms and a small hump on the body. Size is generally 4–6 cm. In a proper aquarium they can live 4–5 years.
